title: SOLID: interface segregation and dependency inversion

videos.script: The last lesson asked who changes a piece of code. This one asks who uses it, and who it depends on. {{title}} First, a kiosk that only searches the catalogue. To test it with a stand-in, Python demands five methods it never calls. {{kiosk}} Interface segregation says a client should depend only on what it uses. Split the promises, and the reference book from lesson 3 stops claiming it can be lent. {{split}} One library object, three small roles, and a test double one method long. {{roles}} Then dependency inversion. The rules about overdue fines should not import the mail code. The rules declare what they need, a notifier, and the mail code fits it. {{inversion}} You will see the direction of every dependency, read straight off the import lines. {{imports}} That idea, applied to a whole program, has a name: ports and adapters. {{ports}} And at the end, the warning. The same fine, written with six classes and with one function. A principle is worth applying when you can name the change it waits for. {{overdone}}
